_about: Every tunable number used by the adjudication engine lives here and nowhere else. Each carries the reason it has this value. If asked 'why 98.5%?', point at this file. Values are defaults chosen from published practice for the MiFish 12S fish marker, NOT tuned to make any particular sample pass.

min_length.why: The MiFish amplicon is about 160-190 bp. A fragment under 100 bp covers too little of the variable region to separate close species, so it is dropped as a short fragment.

max_n_percent.why: N means the sequencer could not call the base. More than 2% N in a ~150 bp read is 3+ uncalled bases inside the region we use to tell species apart.

min_mean_quality.why: Q20 is a 1% expected error rate per base, the usual floor for amplicon reads. Only applied to FASTQ input; FASTA has no quality scores, and that is stated in the output.

min_complexity_entropy.why: Shannon entropy of base composition. Below 1.5 bits the read is dominated by one or two letters (poly-A, repeats) and is not a real mitochondrial fragment.

min_read_count.why: A distinct sequence seen exactly once is overwhelmingly a PCR or sequencing error variant of a real sequence. Dropping singletons is standard denoising practice.

identity_floor.why: Below 80% to every reference entry the sequence is not recognisably a fish 12S fragment at all (even distant fish families stay above this). It is dropped as 'unrelated', not queued.

identity_species.why: Species-level call needs at least 98.5% identity to the best reference. 12S fish studies commonly use 98-99%; 98.5% sits in the middle.

min_species_margin.why: If the best species and the best DIFFERENT species are within 1 identity point, the sequence cannot honestly be called to one species. It goes to the review queue as ambiguous.

human_identity.why: MiFish primers also amplify human 12S. A read at or above 95% to the human mitogenome is treated as human contamination and dropped.

unknown_max_confidence.why: An unknown can never be shown as confirmed. Its confidence is capped here so that it cannot be mistaken for a species call, however good its closest match looks.

confidence_max_known.why: No call is ever shown as 100% certain: the reference list is finite and a perfect match to a wrong entry is still possible.

min_detection_reads.why: Species backed by fewer than 10 reads in a sample are reported as 'trace' and not as a detection. Index hopping and tag-jumping routinely produce a handful of stray reads.

retake_min_kept_fraction.why: Below 10% usable the library is essentially a failed PCR (90% junk), so resample. Earlier this was 50%, but running real deep-sequenced estuary samples showed that 70% off-target reads (e.g. 100,000 good fish reads among 400,000) is a caution, not a reason to discard a sample that still has plenty of valid data. The absolute read count below is the main test.

caution_max_dropped_fraction.why: Between 25% and 50% of reads lost is not unusable, but it says the library was poor (for example primer-dimer). The verdict is 'Usable with caution' and the loss is shown, instead of pretending nothing happened.

retake_min_kept_reads.why: Fewer than 1,000 usable reads cannot describe a community: a species at 0.5% would have 5 reads. This is the main 'unusable' test.

share_tolerance_factor.why: Amplification bias between species is real (published work on this dataset reports a positive but imperfect read-to-DNA relationship). An estimated share within 3-fold of the source-supported share is called consistent; outside it is flagged.

season_months.why: Documented rule that maps a collection month to a season. Pearl River Delta: wet, hot monsoon summer is Apr-Sep, the dry cool winter is Oct-Mar. Change here for another region.

alert_latency_seconds.why: The brief wants an alert 'within seconds' of a triggering sample being processed; the alert event records its measured latency and this is the budget it is judged against.
